title: One member buys Plus and the partner expects it immediately
preconditions: A and B are active members of one space on the Free plan.
B keeps the app open and checks storage limits.

actions.note: A completes a verified Plus purchase.
B checks the current storage limit.

expected_behavior: Plus is Space-level; both members read the same authoritative entitlement row.
B observes the higher media ceiling after the entitlement is applied, not merely after the store sheet closes.
A failed or delayed webhook does not grant Plus on the client alone.
candidate_failure_modes: B sees Free limits indefinitely with no explanation.
The client grants Plus from local purchase state while the server still says Free.
A second purchase is required for the partner.
existing_test_coverage: packages/api/src/__tests__/routes/session-plus.test.ts:141 — valid webhook activates Plus for the purchaser Space; partner reads the same state

observed_code_behavior: Plus is a Space-level entitlement: one row is shared by both active members.
The Free media ceiling is 250 MiB and the Plus ceiling is 5 GiB; future-letter allowance differs by plan.
The backend entitlement row is authoritative; client local purchase state cannot grant features.
Verified webhook deliveries are deduplicated and stale events cannot regress a newer state.
Us and Memories are intentionally separate destinations; sky photos are not dated memories.
Free and Plus see the same relationship home.

hypothetical_user_behavior: A fictional participant (Vera Lind) said: "We are auditing Aoi for things that do not need to exist. Walk through Plus and storage as you actually used them: the paywall, plan explanation, storage meter, manage-subscription link, upgrade prompts, feature gates, and every line of copy around them. For each one, ask out loud: "Why does this even exist?" Then say what would break if it were removed, and what it cost you. Name the three most useless things and the one thing you would keep. Do not propose a redesign; remove."

A fictional participant (Vera Lind) said: "I took the wrong path on purpose, twice, and wrote everything down.

Three things I would remove outright:

1) **The storage meter.** It exists to sell me a ceiling I will never touch. I uploaded ~400 screenshots to hit it deliberately. What happened: a bar went amber, then a banner told me to "manage my plan." Nothing else. No feature stopped working, no data was lost, nothing broke in a month of ignoring it. Cost to me: one evening of "am I about to run out of space?" anxiety, plus a help article that says "storage" without ever stating units or what counts against it. Remove the dial and the banner; leave one sentence in the plan table — "X GB included, and here is what counts." That is not a redesign, that is a deletion with a footnote.

2) **The upgrade prompt that fires on the exact feature that just failed.** It appeared over a retry I was mid-way through, with no close affordance visible at my text size, and it ate the draft I had typed. A failed action must preserve my input; instead it harvested my frustration as a conversion event. Remove it entirely. If a feature is gated, say so at the point of use, inline, in the same sentence as the control — not in a modal that traps.

3) **The "progress" bar on plan setup.** It animated to 60%, sat there, and then finished instantly. It was not measuring anything; it was measuring how long I could be made to wait. Fake progress is a lie told at 0.4 seconds per frame. Delete it and show nothing — an honest blank is better than a decorative lie.

The one thing I would keep: **the manage-subscription link.** It is the only control in the entire flow that answered the question I actually had, it went to the right place on the first tap, and the copy on the destination page matched the copy on the link. Consistency like that is rare enough in this app that I want to protect it.

Also, for the record: "Plus," "Pro," and "Premium" appear in three different places with three different descriptions and no way to tell which one I am on. I had to guess. The app should never make me guess."
Vera Lind assumes: the app should never make me guess
Vera Lind assumes: a failed action must preserve my input
Wolf Adler assumes: a spinner is not a status
Wolf Adler assumes: a code field should accept a pasted message
